clue.text: To go down on record describing doctor's round

parts.note: on means onward, as in 'and so on', which can equally be said 'and so forth'

indicators.note: to describe a circle is to trace a line round something, so the record goes round the next two pieces

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: A GP's daily circuit of patients is about to be written down in the official minutes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' is the container signal, in its geometry sense of drawing round something. In British football a club heading for relegation to a lower division is said to be this.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom from sport: a team about to be relegated, sinking to a lower division, is described this way.

clue.text: It may make one look better to deal with stuff

definitions.text: It may make one look better

parts.note: to face a problem is to deal with it
to stuff a bag is to pack it full

explanation.surface: A problem may seem less daunting once somebody has actually tackled the things involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stuff' reads as a noun for things in general, but here it is a verb meaning to cram.
explanation.definitionFit: Example by description: a cosmetic mask spread on the skin to cleanse and tone it, used to improve the complexion.

clue.text: Endure all if endurance embodies existence?

indicators.note: embodies says the four words before it hold the answer within their run of letters

explanation.surface: A stoic's motto: put up with everything, if putting up with things is what being alive amounts to.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym in the everyday sense: what people actually live through, as opposed to fiction or fantasy.

clue.text: I pick a horse up on country trip

indicators.note: in a down entry, on means the first part sits on top of the second
in a down entry, up means the pieces before it are written from bottom to top

parts.note: to cull is to pick out, to select from a group
H is slang for heroin, which is also called horse
a nation is a country

explanation.surface: A rider collects a mount to go hacking through the fields.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns I CULL A H into HALLUCI, and 'on' places that above NATION. 'trip' looks like a ride in the countryside but is the drug sense, as is 'horse'.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang sense: a drug-induced experience of seeing things that are not there is called this.

clue.text: It's very easy, without doctor, to have a stroke

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the first piece goes outside the others

parts.note: a doddle is British slang for something very easy
a GP is a general practitioner, a family doctor

explanation.surface: With no medic on hand, falling seriously ill is all too simple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is the container signal, in its old sense of outside rather than lacking. 'stroke' is not the medical emergency the surface suggests but a way of swimming.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: a simple swimming style with the head above water, the limbs moving as a pet's would.

clue.text: 0-0 draw in united match? Better than that!

indicators.note: to draw in is to pull inside, so the two round letters take the next piece between them

parts.note: the two noughts of the scoreline are written as two letter Os
Utd is how United is abbreviated in football club names and fixture lists

explanation.surface: A football fan hopes Manchester United manage more than a goalless stalemate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw in' is the container signal: the scoreline's two noughts take UTD between them. 'Better' reads as an adjective in the surface but is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a verb: to surpass or exceed what somebody else has achieved.

clue.text: Cold leading to rough throat

indicators.note: leading to puts the first piece in front of the second

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap
raw can mean rough or unrefined, as in raw material or a raw deal

explanation.surface: A winter chill brings on a sore, scratchy gullet.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: strictly a bird's crop, used figuratively for the gullet, as in something sticking there.

clue.text: Simple game with short piece of wood

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a game

indicators.note: short means the following word loses its last letter

parts.note: a stick is a piece of wood

explanation.surface: An easy pastime played with a little bit of timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' drops the K from STICK. RU, for rugby union, is the standard crossword 'game'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: plain and unsophisticated in a countryside way.

clue.text: Cheshire town with one capsized ship

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: a capsized boat is upside down, so in a down entry the word is written bottom to top

parts.note: to ship goods is to send them

explanation.surface: A place in north-west England has a single overturned vessel in its dock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capsized' turns SEND into DNES. 'ship' is a verb, to dispatch. The answer is an industrial town on the River Mersey in north-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Example by location: a town on the Mersey that has been in the county of Cheshire since 1974.

clue.text: Tea dance stopped half way through

indicators.note: stopping at the half-way point leaves only the first half of the dance's name

parts.note: a Latin American ballroom dance whose name is one syllable said twice

explanation.surface: An afternoon social with dancing and refreshments is called off at the midpoint.
explanation.walkthrough: A tea dance is a real afternoon event, so the first two words read as one phrase; they must be split.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: an informal British word for the drink, borrowed from Chinese.

clue.text: On one form of deism it's allowed

parts.note: in cricket the on side of the field is also called the leg side
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: a form of something is a version of it, so the letters that follow take a new arrangement

parts.note: it, with the 's read as 'is' joining to the definition

explanation.surface: A commentator notes that a particular branch of rational religion is tolerated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form of' rearranges DEISM IT into TIMISED. In cricket, 'on' and 'leg' name the same side of the field, the one behind the batter's legs.
explanation.definitionFit: Near-synonym as a past participle: made lawful, given official permission.

clue.text: It can pull some objects, potentially deflecting aim

indicators.note: potentially says the letters of the two words after it could become something else

explanation.surface: Some force tugs at things and may knock a marksman's shot off target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potentially' is the anagram signal for 'deflecting aim'. The whole clue also describes the answer well, since such a force can throw a compass or projectile off line.
explanation.definitionFit: Description from physics: the region of force round a magnet that attracts iron and steel.

clue.text: Rice dish gets very good praise, though unfinished

parts.note: pi is short for pious, old slang for very good in a sanctimonious way

indicators.note: unfinished means the word for praise loses its last letter

parts.note: to laud is to praise

explanation.surface: A restaurant's biryani earns warm compliments even though the diner left some.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' drops the D from LAUD. PI, from pious, is a crossword regular for 'very good'.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: spiced grains cooked in stock, of Middle Eastern and Indian origin.

clue.text: Perhaps one is glad to get by

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the three words after it could be something else, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Somebody is maybe happy just to scrape through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is the anagram signal for 'one is glad'. 'to get by' reads as one phrase meaning to manage, but only its last word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym as a preposition: next to, beside, as in a house standing by the river.

clue.text: Ancient bloke keeps going home with date

indicators.note: keeps means holds, so the word for bloke holds the other pieces inside it

parts.note: a codger is a fellow, usually an old one
going in the sense of leaving: 'I'm off' means 'I'm going'
in means at home

explanation.surface: A very old chap still sets off back to his house with a girlfriend on his arm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeps' is the container signal. The answer is jocular, rather rude British slang for a very old person, and 'Ancient' is a noun here, not an adjective describing the bloke.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang synonym: a disrespectful British term for an elderly person, pictured as evading the grave.

clue.text: Random outcome, heading off in boat

indicators.note: in places the shortened word inside the word for boat

parts.note: a dory is a small flat-bottomed fishing boat

indicators.note: heading off means the first letter of the word for outcome is removed

parts.note: a result is an outcome

explanation.surface: Nobody can predict what happens when a small craft sets out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' leaves ESULT, which 'in' places within the boat. 'Random outcome' reads as one phrase but splits between definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Near-synonym: lacking any plan or method, jumping from one thing to another.

clue.text: Stocky man with a scruffy vest outside yard

parts.note: he is the pronoun for a man

indicators.note: outside says the rearranged word goes round the abbreviation that follows
scruffy means untidy, so the letters of the next word are disordered

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for yard, the unit of length

explanation.surface: A thickset fellow in a tatty singlet stands out in the back garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scruffy' rearranges VEST and 'outside' wraps it round Y, giving VYSET. In Britain a vest is an undershirt and a yard is a paved area behind a house.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: solidly and broadly built.

clue.text: Nasty, but it won't start to block my passage

indicators.note: something that blocks a passage sits inside it, so the shortened word goes inside the exclamation

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, as is 'my!'

indicators.note: a word that won't start is missing its first letter

parts.note: horrid means nasty

explanation.surface: Something unpleasant refuses to get going and obstruct my way through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'my' is not a possessive but an exclamation of surprise. 'but it won't start' leaves ORRID, which 'to block' places inside that exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a long hallway with rooms opening off it.

clue.text: Noise that larks circling parrot find attractive

indicators.note: circling means the jumbled letters go round the bird that follows
to lark is to frolic about, so the two words before it are jumbled

parts.note: a kea is a large green New Zealand parrot

explanation.surface: Songbirds wheeling round a caged macaw rather like the sound it makes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'larks' is a verb here, not the birds the surface shows: it jumbles two words into TASHINETO, and 'circling' wraps that round the parrot.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to develop a liking for a person or thing.

clue.text: Lost? Put on a little light

parts.note: to put on weight or extra staff is to add it
an LED, a light-emitting diode, is a tiny light

explanation.surface: Someone who cannot find the way switches on a small torch.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: muddled and confused, unable to think straight.

clue.text: Tribesman wants wild area

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A member of a clan longs for untamed open country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges WANTS into TSWAN. The answer is a member of the main people of Botswana.
explanation.definitionFit: Example by membership: one of a Bantu people of southern Africa, chiefly Botswana.

clue.text: Axe is next to spade — sorry about that

indicators.note: about means the word for sorry goes round the other two pieces

parts.note: sorry as an adjective means wretched, as in a sorry state

indicators.note: next to puts the first piece directly beside the second

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for spades in card games

explanation.surface: A gardener apologises for leaving a chopper lying beside a shovel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Axe' is the sacking, as in getting the axe, and 'sorry' is an adjective, not an apology. 'about' is the container signal and 'next to' joins the two inner pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative synonym: the sack, removal from a job.

clue.text: A little rusty, like needles

indicators.note: A little says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some old sewing pins have gone slightly brown with corrosion.
explanation.definitionFit: Example in the plural: the pointed pieces that track a record's groove on a turntable.

clue.text: Note gun's provided with recoil?

indicators.note: a recoil is a springing back, so the pieces before it are read from right to left

parts.note: to gun an engine is to rev it
provided means if, as in 'provided you agree'

explanation.surface: A memo records whether the firearm comes with a kickback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with recoil' turns REV IF into the answer. 'gun' is a verb, what a driver does to an engine. The answer is a British five-pound banknote.
explanation.definitionFit: Example of the category: the informal British name for a five-pound banknote.

clue.text: Memorise poet — Byron, possibly Lawrence

parts.note: Edward Lear wrote nonsense verse such as The Owl and the Pussycat

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of the name before it may be put another way

parts.note: T. E. Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia, is known by his initials

explanation.surface: A student commits a writer's verse to memory, perhaps Lord Byron's or D. H. Lawrence's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges BYRON into NBYRO. The surface suggests D. H. Lawrence, who wrote poetry, but the initials needed are those of Lawrence of Arabia.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym phrase: to commit to memory through sheer repetition.

clue.text: Ditch water in some red earth

indicators.note: to ditch something is to throw it away, so the word for water is discarded from the two words run together

parts.note: a mere is a lake, a stretch of water

explanation.surface: Stagnant drainage water lies in a patch of rust-coloured soil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ditch' is a verb, not a trench: run 'some red' together and throw out MERE. Ditchwater is a single idea in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Near-synonym: a piece of turf, the ground with its grass.

clue.text: Expensive letter opener

definitions.meaning: the word that begins the greeting of a letter, before the recipient's name

explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: an adjective for costly, and the conventional first word of written correspondence.

clue.text: Corrupt Tory edict limits one who oversees business news?

indicators.note: limits means sets bounds around, so the rearranged letters enclose the next piece
to corrupt something is to spoil or alter it, so the letters of the next two words are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A crooked decree from a Conservative government muzzles a financial journalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'limits' looks like a verb restricting the journalist, but it wraps the nine letters jumbled by 'Corrupt' round one more. The City is London's financial district, which gives the job its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Job description: the British newspaper journalist in charge of the financial pages.
